claims.text: Optimized thermomechanical processing produces a homogeneous microstructure in the alloy.
The coupled tribo-corrosion response is governed by the balance between mechanical removal of the native passive oxide and electrochemical repassivation.
Sliding mechanically removes the protective oxide film from the alloy surface.
CoCrFeMnNi can rapidly reform its passive oxide after mechanical removal.
When repassivation outpaces wear-driven film removal, an effective corrosion-protective barrier is maintained.
When wear-driven film removal outpaces repassivation, localized passive-film breakdown increases overall degradation.
The relative rates of passive-film removal and regrowth control the surface's exposure to corrosive attack.
At moderate sliding speeds and loads, repassivation kinetics are sufficient to preserve protection.
Under moderate sliding conditions, wear degradation will be lower than under isolated wear in an inert environment.
Under moderate sliding conditions, corrosion degradation will be lower than under static corrosion without sliding.
Increasing sliding severity until film removal exceeds repassivation will increase degradation.
At extremely high sliding speeds or loads, mechanical damage will overwhelm repassivation and the proposed protective effect will fail.
The balance between film removal and repassivation may vary with local microstructure and experimental setup.
Passive-film thickness, electrochemical current or potential, and wear-scar geometry can be measured while sliding speed and load are varied.
A lack of association between sliding severity, passive-film dynamics, and degradation would falsify the proposed governing mechanism.
